{{Cheatsheet}}

Git is a distributed version control system that tracks changes to files and coordinates work between people on the same codebase.

New to Git? [https://learngitbranching.js.org/ Learn Git Branching] is a visual, interactive tutorial; [https://git-scm.com/book/en/v2 Pro Git] is the free, thorough book.

== Basic example: clone, edit, commit, push ==

<syntaxhighlight lang="bash" line highlight="5,6,7" copy>
git clone https://github.com/user/repo.git
cd repo
git switch -c my-feature          # branch off main
# ... edit files ...
git add .                         # stage all changes
git commit -m "Add my feature"    # snapshot them
git push -u origin my-feature     # share on the remote, remember upstream
</syntaxhighlight>

Every change follows the same loop: '''edit → stage (<syntaxhighlight lang="bash" inline>git add</syntaxhighlight>) → commit → push'''. The '''working tree''' is what you edit, the '''index''' is what you stage, the remote is where you share.

== Setup ==

<syntaxhighlight lang="bash" copy>
git config --global user.name "Ada Lovelace"
git config --global user.email ada@example.com
git config --global init.defaultBranch main
git config --global alias.co checkout     # `git co` works from now on
git config --global pull.rebase true      # pull = fetch + rebase
</syntaxhighlight>

{| class="wikitable"
! Command !! Effect
|-
| <syntaxhighlight lang="bash" inline>git config --global user.name "Ada"</syntaxhighlight> || who you are, for every repo — needed before the first commit
|-
| <syntaxhighlight lang="bash" inline>git config --global init.defaultBranch main</syntaxhighlight> || new repos default to main
|-
| <syntaxhighlight lang="bash" inline>git config --global alias.co checkout</syntaxhighlight> || create a short alias
|-
| <syntaxhighlight lang="bash" inline>git config --global --list</syntaxhighlight> || show all config
|}

'''Start a repository:'''

<syntaxhighlight lang="bash" copy>
git init                # new repo in the current directory
git init my-project     # ... in a subdirectory
git clone <url>         # copy an existing repository
git clone <url> dir     # ... into a given directory
</syntaxhighlight>

== Daily workflow ==

<syntaxhighlight lang="bash" copy>
git status                  # what changed?
git diff                    # unstaged changes
git diff --staged           # staged changes
git add file.py             # stage one file
git add .                   # stage all changes
git add -p                  # stage hunks interactively
git commit -m "Fix typo"    # commit the staged changes
git commit -am "Fix typo"   # stage tracked changes + commit in one go
</syntaxhighlight>

<blockquote>
'''<syntaxhighlight lang="bash" inline>git commit -am</syntaxhighlight> only stages ''tracked'' files.''' A brand-new file is untracked and still needs an explicit <syntaxhighlight lang="bash" inline>git add</syntaxhighlight>.
</blockquote>

== Inspecting history ==

<syntaxhighlight lang="bash" copy>
git log --oneline                   # one line per commit
git log --oneline --graph --all     # branch topology
git log -p                          # full diffs
git log --follow -- file.py         # history of a single file
git show <hash>                     # one commit in detail
git blame file.py                   # who changed each line
</syntaxhighlight>

== Branching & merging ==

<syntaxhighlight lang="bash" copy>
git branch                  # list local branches
git branch -a               # include remote-tracking branches
git branch feature-branch   # create a copy of current branch named feature-branch and switch to it
git branch main-backup main # create a copy of main named main-backup and switch to it
git switch -c feature-branch  # = branch feature-branch + switch to it
git switch -c main-backup main # = git branch main-backup main + switch to it
git switch feature          # switch to an existing branch
git switch -                # switch back to the previous branch
git merge feature           # merge feature into the current branch
git branch -d feature       # delete a merged branch
git branch -D feature       # force-delete an unmerged branch
</syntaxhighlight>

<blockquote>
'''Git before 2.23 has no <syntaxhighlight lang="bash" inline>git switch</syntaxhighlight> / <syntaxhighlight lang="bash" inline>git restore</syntaxhighlight>.'''
Use <syntaxhighlight lang="bash" inline>git checkout -b feature</syntaxhighlight> to branch, <syntaxhighlight lang="bash" inline>git checkout feature</syntaxhighlight> to switch, and <syntaxhighlight lang="bash" inline>git checkout -- file.py</syntaxhighlight> to discard changes.
</blockquote>

== Rebase ==

First create a backup of the branch to be rebased: 
<syntaxhighlight lang="bash" copy>
git branch main-backup main # main-backup is an exact copy of main
git switch main # switches back to target the main branch
</syntaxhighlight>

<syntaxhighlight lang="bash" copy>
git rebase main          # replays current branch on top of main
git rebase -i HEAD~3     # interactively reorganises the last 3 commits on current branch
</syntaxhighlight>

== Merge conflicts ==

<syntaxhighlight lang="bash" copy>
# git status shows "both modified"; files contain markers:
#   <<<<<<< HEAD  ...  =======  ...  >>>>>>> feature
# edit the file to keep the right lines, then:
git add <resolved files>
git commit              # after a merge
git rebase --continue   # after a rebase
git merge --abort       # back out of the merge entirely
git rebase --abort      # ... or of the rebase
</syntaxhighlight>

== Remotes ==

<syntaxhighlight lang="bash" copy>
git remote -v                    # list remotes
git remote add <remote name:e.g., origin> <url>      # connect a remote
git fetch <remote name>               # download commits, don't touch your work
git pull                         # fetch + merge
git push                         # upload your commits
git push -u origin feature       # first push of a branch: set upstream
git push origin --delete feature # delete a branch on the remote
git tag v1.0                     # tag the current commit
git push origin v1.0             # share the tag
</syntaxhighlight>

<blockquote>
'''pull is fetch + merge.''' It can create merge commits. Prefer a linear history with <syntaxhighlight lang="bash" inline>git pull --rebase</syntaxhighlight>, or set it once with <syntaxhighlight lang="bash" inline>git config --global pull.rebase true</syntaxhighlight>.
</blockquote>

== Undoing ==

<syntaxhighlight lang="bash" copy>
git restore file.py                    # discard unstaged changes to a file
git restore --staged file.py           # unstage a file
git commit --amend                     # fix the last commit (message / forgotten file)
git reset HEAD~1                       # undo the last commit, unstage the changes
git reset --soft HEAD~1                # undo the last commit, keep changes staged
git reset --hard HEAD~1                # undo the last commit and drop everything
git revert <hash>                      # undo a commit that is already pushed
</syntaxhighlight>

<blockquote>
'''<syntaxhighlight lang="bash" inline>git reset --hard</syntaxhighlight> can be destructive:''' it trashes the resetted commit ''and'' uncommitted edits. 

However, partial recovery immediately after accidental trigger is possible. 

<syntaxhighlight lang="bash" copy>
git reflog              # lists previous HEAD locations 
</syntaxhighlight>

Expected output:

<pre>
abc1234 HEAD@{0}: reset: moving to HEAD~3
def5678 HEAD@{1}: commit: Latest work you want back
</pre>

Recover committed changes
<syntaxhighlight lang="bash" copy>
git reset --hard "HEAD@{1}" # reset once more to the desired commit just before reset.
</syntaxhighlight>

Attempt to recover staged changes:
<syntaxhighlight lang="bash" copy>
git fsck --unreachable      # search for dangling tip objects (often leftovers from reset --hard)
</syntaxhighlight>

Changes to untracked files are normally kept on disk. Unstaged changes to tracked files are '''permanently lost'''.
</blockquote>

<blockquote>
'''<code>amend</code> rewrites history''' (new commit hashes). Normally, it should only be used on local commits that are not yet shared.
</blockquote>

== Stash ==

Put uncommitted work aside to switch branches, then bring it back. Stashes are not tied to a branch — a stack you can pop anywhere.

<syntaxhighlight lang="bash" copy>
git stash              # stash tracked changes
git stash -u           # also stash untracked files
git stash -m "WIP"     # stash with a message
git stash list         # see what is stashed
git stash show -p      # inspect the newest stash's diff
</syntaxhighlight>

'''pop vs apply''' — pop restores and drops the stash; apply restores and keeps it:

<syntaxhighlight lang="bash" copy>
git stash pop              # restore newest stash, then drop it
git stash apply            # restore, keep the stash
git stash apply stash@{1}  # restore a specific stash
git stash drop stash@{1}   # delete a specific stash
git stash clear            # delete all stashes
git stash branch fix       # new branch at the stash point, pop onto it
</syntaxhighlight>

<blockquote>
'''Untracked files are left behind by default.''' <syntaxhighlight lang="bash" inline>git stash</syntaxhighlight> only stashes ''tracked'' changes — a brand-new file survives in the working tree. Add <syntaxhighlight lang="bash" inline>-u</syntaxhighlight> for untracked files too, or <syntaxhighlight lang="bash" inline>-a</syntaxhighlight> to also include ignored files.
</blockquote>

<blockquote>
'''A conflicting pop keeps the stash.''' Restoring onto a branch that changed the same lines leaves the stash in place: resolve like a merge conflict, then <syntaxhighlight lang="bash" inline>git stash drop</syntaxhighlight> once the work is safely committed.
</blockquote>
